……广告团队，他们去发明了所有这些产品，因为你在广告平台上做的每一件小事都有一个SKU、一个损益表、一个……因为你有大量产品，所以（听不清01:10:11）成功了。第二个问题是，他们说范围实际上是输入，而不是输出。我们和经理谈话时说：“嗯，这个人的范围管理得很棒。他们应该得到晋升。”然后他们会说：“但你给了他们那个范围。我们应该评判你，而不是那个人。我们怎么判断他们如何利用那个范围呢？”这其实有很大的不同。第三个问题是，在几乎每个团队中，我们一些最优秀的人都在处理范围不确定的项目。这些是高风险项目。我们还不知道这个东西能否成功，或者会不会失败，Mike会不会取消项目。如果我们只建立一个奖励范围的系统，就会严重打击人们去尝试这些更具创意、风险更高的项目的积极性。（01:10:52）所以我们陷入了困境。然后我们尝试了很多框架，最终选定了PSHE这个框架，它来自我的老导师[听不清01:10:01]Clark，他曾是我在微软多年的上司。PSHE代表问题、解决方案、方法、执行。说实话，我曾多次尝试想出一个更好的缩写词，但始终未能成功。所以就用“push”这个词。这是我能想到的最好的了。但这里是如何运作的……如果你是一名初级产品经理，发生什么呢？你接到一个问题。你接到一个解决方案。你接到一个方法。“去和那个人谈谈。写这份文件。开这个会议”等等。你只需要执行，按照这个流程来做，这就是我们对你的期望。当你晋升到更高职位时，我们给你一个问题和一个粗略的解决方案。你要自己想出方法。你要想：“我们该如何组织这个项目？有哪些里程碑？如何将它推向市场？如何安排会议？有哪些流程？”所有这些都在“H”中体现出来。（01:11:03）在某个阶段，你晋升到更高职位。我们给你一个问题，你回来后给出解决方案。我们根据解决方案的创造力和有效性来评判你。在某个阶段，你足够资深，可以告诉我们问题所在，比如：“嘿，我知道你让我去处理激活问题，但实际上我认为我们的核心问题是品牌”，或者“我认为我们的核心问题是质量”，或者“……”。这就是这种思维方式的巅峰。（01:11:27）现在回到这张图，发生的一个有趣现象是，各个团队在两个维度上对自己进行评估，最终在两者之间形成了曲线关系。不是线性的，而是逐渐变化的。在职业生涯早期，大多数人处于E点，你接到问题和解决方案，接到方法，然后执行，范围逐渐扩大。职业生涯后期，同样，你处于P级别，你做越来越大的产品。而作为创业者、CEO、所有者等的职责，就是做越来越大的项目。但在中间阶段，斜率发生变化，突然间，重点不再是范围，而是PSHE了。
文中有一处提到“trough of dissolution”，我暂且将其翻译为“解体低谷期”。（01:12:14）：之所以这么称呼，是因为……我暂停分享，让我们来探讨一下这个阶段的具体情况。我曾就此与校准委员会进行过交流。我们之所以将其称为解体低谷期，是因为对员工而言，这是一个令人困惑的时期。从高中到大学，人们一直专注于“范围”相关的能力。但到了这个阶段，突然被告知“我们不再以‘范围’为评判标准，而是转向PSHE这种令人费解的维度”。对校准人员或管理者而言，这同样令人困惑，因为职级之间的差异可能不再取决于“范围”——他们或许从事着完全相同的工作，但关键在于工作方式的差异。这里有个例子：三级职位和七级职位的差距可能并非在于“范围”，他们可能从事着完全相同的工作，但关键在于工作方式的差异。（01:12:56）：因此，PSHE思维模式成为一个难以突破的框架。事实证明，这种人才评估方式并非产品管理领域独有。以工程师和设计师为例，评估标准通常基于任务完成率——将销售人员按达成率排名即可。但以销售人员为例，评估标准往往基于任务达成率。但若深入探讨，你会发现人们真正看重的是销售人员对任务难度的把控能力，以及如何选择合适的市场区域。真正优秀的销售人员往往具备以下特质：能够开拓新领域，识别核心问题，解决难题。（01:13:45）：这种思维模式与PSHE理念高度契合。优秀的销售人员必须能够进入新领域，识别核心问题并解决难题。这也启发我将其应用于多元化人才评估体系。研究发现，“P型思维者”（善于识别核心问题，解决复杂问题的群体）与出色的提问能力高度相关。他们能精准发现核心问题，评估优先级，作出关键决策。这也成为我评估人才价值的主要框架。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. There's so much there. A couple quick questions. Is this basically your calibration ladder framework for PMs at this point? And then is this also just like your interview guide, just interview at each of these pieces to level the person?
turns.zh: 哇。这里内容真多。我有几个快速的问题。这基本上是你们目前针对产品经理的能力评估框架吗？然后这也是你们的面试指南吗？就是针对每个模块进行面试来评估候选人能力？

turns.speaker: Shishir Mehrotra
turns.en: Yeah. So it's definitely how we do. Our version of leveling is PSHE, and we use a set of Radford levels. Radford has this really interesting way of describing that as you grow in a profession... He uses the analogy of someone, of a sailor and that a junior sailor is learning to tie knots and then you gradually can tie all the standard knots and then you can tie the advanced knots and so on, and so you work your way up and at some point the way you're judged is you invented nylon and there's list between there. It's like a way to evaluate every role. It's very similar to PSHE. And so we look at a similar list. But yeah, basically all of our roles are evaluated on something that corresponds with PSHE. (01:15:17): And in terms of interviews, yeah, you look for the same thing. And by the way, I should say interviewing is one part of this. And you talk about interviewing. You talk about calibration. There's one other really important one which is reference checking. And I think the best way to assess PSHE is actually through references. And so the most important guide we write isn't the interview guide. When we call this person's references, what do you ask to actually get at these questions? Because people can often confuse them. (01:15:46): Just to pick product managers as an example. We all know some really amazing H level product managers. And one of the reasons, one of the hallmarks, of an H level product manager is that their counterparts usually love them and they'll say things like, "Oh, my gosh. The person runs such efficient meetings and all the communication is always clear. [inaudible 01:16:07] always buttoned up. Execs know what we're doing. The market knows what we're doing. Sales team know what we're doing." That's great H. And then you'll ask them a question about, "Okay. So when you're deciding which problem to solve, who is the leader of that? And are they picking the right problems? Or when there's a hard problem, who is regularly coming up with the best solutions for them? Who do you turn to? Who is the most obvious person to turn to say, 'This is really hard problem. What's the right solution?'?" (01:16:31): An amazing number of people will tell you, "No, they run a great meeting but actually solving the problem, designer does that," or, "What are the problems? No. The CEO tells us what to do. That's not what this person's really good at. Yeah. I'm not sure we're solving the right problem, but boy, we run a great meeting." And it's not meant to diminish any of that. I mean, we spent a while talking about rituals, which mostly happen at that H level, so I don't think it's unimportant, but it's actually quite hard to assess in an interview but incredibly easy to assess in a reference check. And I think getting good at that is really important.
turns.zh: 是的。这确实是我们的做法。我们版本的能力评估体系叫PSHE，使用的是拉德福德（Radford）等级标准。拉德福德用了一个很有趣的比喻来描述职业成长过程……他用水手作为类比——初级水手学习打结，逐渐掌握标准打结技巧，再到高级打结技巧，最终达到发明尼龙等成就。整个过程就像评估每个职位的标准。这和PSHE非常相似。所以我们参考了类似的评估列表。基本上，我们所有职位的评估都与PSHE对应。（01:15:17）：至于面试部分，是的，我们寻找的能力是相同的。顺便说一下，面试只是其中一部分。你们提到面试和能力评估，但还有一个非常重要的环节——背景调查。实际上评估PSHE的最佳方式就是通过背景调查。因此我们写的最重要的指南不是面试指南。当我们联系候选人推荐人时，到底要问哪些问题才能触及关键？因为人们往往容易混淆这些概念。（01:15:46）：以产品经理为例。我们都知道一些非常出色的H级产品经理。H级产品经理的标志之一是他们的同行非常喜欢他们，评价他们说：“天哪，这个人开会效率超高，沟通总是清晰明了。[01:16:07未录音]一切都井井有条。高管们清楚我们的方向。市场也明白我们的策略。销售团队也知道我们的目标。”这就是优秀的H级产品经理。但当你问他们：“在决定解决哪个问题时，谁是项目负责人，他们是否选对了问题？遇到难题时，谁能经常提出最佳解决方案？你会找谁？谁是最明显的求助对象，问‘这问题太难了，正确的解决方案是什么？’？”（01:16:31）很多候选人会说：“不，他们开会很棒，但实际解决问题是设计师做的”，或者“问题在哪？不，CEO告诉我们该做什么。这人真正擅长的不是这个。是啊，我不确定我们是否选对了问题，但开会确实很棒。”这不是贬低他们的能力。我是说，我们花了很多时间讨论仪式感，而这在H级产品经理中很常见，所以我不认为这不重要，但在面试中评估这部分确实很难，但通过背景调查却非常容易评估。我认为掌握这项技能非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You may have mentioned this, but what's the question there? Is there a question that you could recommend?
turns.zh: 你可能提到过这个问题，但具体问题是什么？你能推荐一个问题吗？

turns.speaker: Shishir Mehrotra
turns.en: The absolute ideal case is you get to the person that you're doing the reference check with and you don't even tell them who you're asking about and you just say, "When you think of your teams, who is best at..." And this obviously only works in cases where you have a pretty deep relationship with the person you're getting referenced from and so on. So you can't always do that. But ideally you want to mimic that behavior. One of the things I think that's hard about reference checks is people have... They have perverse incentives in a reference check. They're not really... Some of it is for good reason. Some of it is for bad reason. People generally don't like criticizing people and they also feel judged themselves and they don't want... There's legal reasons that things can blow back and so on. (01:17:55): And so what I try really hard to do is to draw contrasts. So you try to say things... There's a couple of techniques I've used for this. In the best case you say, "I'm not going to even tell you who I'm asking about, but when you think about this team who regularly identifies what problems they should focus on? Who is most reliable at coming up with the solutions to the hardest problems?" And you work your way through it. The other way I like to do it is to provide contrast to give the person an out to not make it obvious to them that I have this ranking. And so I'll say things like, "When you think about this person, and I'll give you four different personas. Someone who's regularly coming up with the problems that the team should be focused on. Someone who given a set of problems is constantly solving them in this really creative way. The person that is just really good at getting a team moving. Or the person who can take a playbook and execute it with high precision and high quality and stuff." (01:18:47): And I won't tell them that I have a qualitative judgment that one is better than the other, but you want them... Because you just want your reference check to talk and you want them to say what's on their mind of... You want to give them an opening to not feel like they're judging. Obviously, another question I always ask people is, "Would you hire this person again? Or how excitedly would you hire this person again?" I always ask them, "What questions should I have asked that I didn't?" Another key technique for reference checks is you just need people to... Once they start talking, they'll reveal what they really feel and often the little things will come out. But for this particular thing, if I want to know where they stand on this axis, don't tell people what you value. By the way, I will say I value P over S over H over E. I've seen many companies that would reverse that scale. And by the way, there's industries where it's very required. You don't want a bunch of people running around and constantly telling you to solve some different problem. I just need people that can do this job that we give them super, super well. And it depends a bit what your personality is and what your company's culture is and so on. So it's not actually that unbelievable that I might value the E over the P. Anybody who knows me, that's probably not true, but for a reference check, you can probably not give that away.
turns.zh:
理想情况下，你找到需要进行背景调查的对象时，甚至不必透露对方的身份，只需问一句：“当你回想起你的团队时，谁最擅长……？”显然，这种方法只有在你与被推荐人关系极为亲密的情况下才行得通。因此并非所有情况都能如此操作，但你应当努力效仿这种沟通方式。  

我认为背景调查中最难处理的问题在于，人们在此过程中存在种种不正当动机。有些是出于善意，有些则另有目的。人们普遍不愿批评他人，也会自我防御，更不愿承担法律风险（比如信息泄露等）。  

为此，我特别注重通过对比来化解矛盾。比如，你可以说：“我甚至不会透露对方的身份，但当你回想起这个团队时，谁最善于发现需要关注的问题？谁最能为最棘手的难题想出解决方案？”  

另一种方法是通过反差对比，让对方无需直面你的排名标准。例如：“当你回想起这个人时，我会给出四个不同的人设：一个能持续发现团队应关注的问题的人；一个面对难题时总能以创新方式解决的人；一个能高效推动团队行动的人；一个能严格执行既定方案的人。”  

我不会透露自己对某人优劣的定性判断，而是通过引导让对方畅谈心得。  

此外，我常问候选人：“你还会再次聘用此人吗？你对其热情度如何？”  

关键技巧在于保持中立：不要主动透露自己的价值观。例如，我会说：“相较于S型、H型和E型，我更看重P型。” 需要注意的是，许多公司会反过来调整这个排序标准，而某些行业对此有明确要求。  

最后，切记背景调查的核心目标：找到能出色完成当前工作的候选人。这取决于你的个性和公司文化等因素。因此，认为E型比P型更重要并非不可思议——熟悉我的人可能知道这不准确，但在背景调查中，你不必暴露真实偏好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. That was gold. I hadn't heard these reference check insights. And so I'm really happy we got to that. Maybe one last question on reference checks. How often do you find that a reference check leads to you not hiring someone, just ballpark? Or is that hard to say?
turns.zh: 哇，真是高明之见。我之前从未听过这些背景调查方面的见解。真高兴我们能探讨到这点。最后再问个关于背景调查的问题。大致说来，背景调查导致你不录用某人的情况有多常见？或者这个问题太难回答了？

turns.speaker: Shishir Mehrotra
turns.en: All the time. And I will say I try to do them as early in the process as practical if it's possible. Because I think it's actually the worst feeling for an interviewee to go through a process and then get dinged at the reference check stage. It's a really crappy experience for the candidate. And obviously you have to be careful about not ruining anything for them. You can't always do the reference check as early as you can. When you're inside a company, when you're inside Google or Facebook or so on, you can generally do them even before you enter. It's an expectation of we're going to hear a little bit about people in that process. And I generally value the reference check over interview signals. If I had to stack rank in interviews what is the best signal, the reference check is the top of the list. Those people, they worked with this person sometimes for years, their knowledge, what you're going to get out of 30 minutes of artificial scenarios, it's just never going to compare with what a good reference check will give you. (01:21:12): And then the second best thing I value is anything that feels like a real work exercise, which is also... Even that is hard because some people, their skillset doesn't naturally lead to a compressed time work exercise. But we do a thing for basically all our roles where at the start of the interview loop, the candidate presents to everyone on the loop and we invite some other people in the company to attend too. For a while it was open the whole company. Now we're big enough where that's not practical. But the original is very simple. At the beginning of the loop, the person presents. And generally for most roles, there's a exercise that they do, but about half the time is spent on them presenting whatever they want. They can talk about themselves. They can teach us something and then another half is we've given them a prompt, something that we want to direct. (01:21:58): One of the things that I think when you're doing interviewing, one way to think about it, I call it home court, away court, neutral court, you want interviews to balance in all those different spheres. So a common mistake people make is they do all questions in home court. "Hey. If you're joining Airbnb, what would you do about X?" And what is the candidate going to say? They clearly can't be as thoughtful as you. They haven't thought about it nearly as much as you have. So really what you're testing is, "Did they come to the same answer that we did?" which is a pretty crappy way to judge someone. Home court questions tend to be tough. You have to be very careful about how you do them. Away court questions can also be tough. This person, you say, "How did you solve this problem?" And they say, "Well, we did this thing." And you don't really know was that problem actually hard? Was it somebody else was telling them what to do? Are they just not telling you the whole story of what happened and so on? (01:22:50): So you try really hard to make... Most of our interviews are done neutral court. So the vast majority [inaudible 01:22:54] teleporter question is a very neutral question. You don't have to know anything about Coda. I don't have to know anything about Airbnb or wherever. I can just ask you this question. But this one thing, the presentation is the away court question. You now have an opportunity to talk about yourself in this new way. And it's super interesting what people do. I mean, I've seen people use that time... I often tell people it's the brag session, but this is like... And for product managers... We do it for every role, but it's like recruiters, salespeople, marketers. (01:23:23): We tell them, "We're going to go through this whole interview process. And at most companies you talk to six different people and six little segments. And at the end of the day you say, 'Gosh. I really wish they had learned this about me.'" And I tell them, "Don't leave this with that feeling. What do you want us to know about you? All our questions are... In some cases we're trying to lower bound you, like, 'How bad could this be?' I want you to upper bound us. I want you to tell us what's really amazing here." And so we'll have the presenter go through that process. And what they choose to talk about is very important. How they choose to present it is very important. But I do it as upper bounding. But if I had to stack rank in interviewing, what do I look for? Reference check at the top, work, product and presentation next, and then all the interviews. When they disagree, that's the order we judge.
turns.zh:
一直如此。我会尽可能在面试流程早期就完成这些环节，因为我认为对面试者来说，经历整个面试过程却在背景调查环节被刷掉是最糟糕的体验。这对候选人来说实在太不公平了。当然，你得注意别给他们带来麻烦。并非所有情况都能尽早进行背景调查。在公司内部，比如在谷歌或Facebook等大公司，通常甚至在面试开始前就能完成背景调查。这是面试流程中预期的环节，面试官会了解候选人过往的工作经历。我认为背景调查比面试中的其他环节更重要。如果要给面试信号排个优先级，背景调查绝对是首选。那些与候选人共事多年的人，他们的见解远比30分钟模拟场景测试更有价值。（01:21:12）  
接下来我重视的第二个环节是模拟实际工作场景的测试。这类测试确实很有挑战性，因为有些候选人的技能组合不适合这种高压环境。不过我们为几乎所有职位都设计了这样的流程：在面试循环开始时，候选人向所有参与者展示项目进展，并邀请公司其他人员参与。起初是全公司开放参与，现在规模太大无法实现，但最初的模式很简单：候选人展示项目，约半数时间用于自由展示，另一半时间则围绕我们设定的场景进行引导式提问。（01:21:58）  
在面试中，我认为平衡不同场景很重要。比如“主场提问”、“客场提问”、“中立提问”。主场提问常有陷阱，比如“如果你加入Airbnb，如何处理X问题？”候选人很难给出和你一样深刻的答案。客场提问同样危险，比如“你是如何解决这个问题的？”对方可能只是照本宣科。中立提问则更中性，比如“如何使用Coda？”无需任何行业背景即可回答。（01:22:50）  
我们尽量保持中立：绝大多数面试采用中立模式。演示环节类似客场提问，候选人有机会以新方式展示自我，观察他们的表现非常有趣。我见过有些人利用这个机会自我吹嘘，但对产品经理来说，这种机会更宝贵。
角色不同，但他们和招聘人员、销售人员、市场营销人员本质上是一样的。（01:23:23）我们会告诉他们：“我们要经历整个面试流程。在大多数公司，你会与六个不同的人交谈，分成六个小环节。到最后，你会感叹‘天哪，我真希望他们能多了解我一点’。” 我会对他们说：“别留下这种遗憾。你们想让我们了解你们什么？我们提出的所有问题……在某些情况下，我们试图给你们设定下限，比如‘情况能有多糟糕？’但我希望你们能给我们设定上限。告诉我们这里真正令人惊叹的地方。” 然后，我们会让面试者经历这个过程。他们选择谈论的内容非常重要，他们的陈述方式也至关重要。但我会把这看作是上限设定。如果要对面试进行排序，优先级最高的应该是背景调查，其次是工作经历、产品展示和最终的面试环节。当他们存在分歧时，我们会按照这个顺序进行评判。
